521.quote_or_event: “We were brothers once, kind to each other, loving each other, wishing well to each other.”
521.explanation: The universal monarch Brahmadatta meets the monk Kitra, his brother in five earlier births, and honours the old bond even though Kitra now owns nothing; Kitra in turn, 'for old friendship's sake', loves the king and counsels him.
521.tie_back: Like the kin in the Kural who keep the old bond with a man who has lost everything, the king does not let Kitra's poverty as a monk cancel their ancient tie.
521.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.5 (see also 13.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
521._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The bond here is between brothers of former births, and the Jain point of the lecture is renunciation rather than the support of kin, so the fit is partial.

522.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra counts vatsalya, loving and guileless affection toward one's fellow believers, among the eight limbs of right faith; the Jain community treats this mutual affection as what keeps the fellowship strong and flourishing.
522.explanation: Vatsalya is the Jain virtue of steady, sincere affection within the community of the faithful, and it is a required limb of samyak darshana.
522.tie_back: The Kural praises kin whose love never fails; vatsalya is the nearest Jain ideal of unfailing affection among one's own, though its circle is the faith community, not blood kin.
522.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara, verses on the eight limbs of right faith (vatsalya-anga) (tr. Champat Rai Jain)
522._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the text; I did not verify the exact verse wording or number in this session. The Kural's promise of growing prosperity from kin has no direct Jain counterpart.

523.quote_or_event: “if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back”
523.explanation: In the list of the ill-behaved monk, Mahavira includes the man who turns on his own friends and maligns them; the same list ends with the one who 'does not share with others'.
523.tie_back: The Kural's man who never mingles heart to heart with his kin lives like a tank without banks; the Jain list likewise marks as failed the man who cuts himself off from those closest to him.
523.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
523._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse is about a monk's conduct toward friends, not kin, and has nothing of the Kural's tank image; next-best match.

524.quote_or_event: After the birth of Mahavira, King Siddhartha and Queen Trisala, whose silver, gold and riches had kept increasing from the time the child was conceived, invite their friends, relations, kinsmen, agnates and cognates, feed them, honour them with flowers, clothes, perfumes and ornaments, and before them name the boy Vardhamana, 'the increasing'.
524.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra shows a prosperous Jain royal household using its increase to gather and honour the whole circle of its kin.
524.tie_back: Valluvar says the fruit of wealth is to be surrounded by one's kin; in the Kalpa Sutra the family's growing wealth is spent precisely on gathering and honouring the kindred.
524.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §§ 104-107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
524._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It is a narrative scene, not a teaching, and Jain doctrine elsewhere stresses that kin cannot save one, so the fit is thematic.

525.quote_or_event: “if he does not share with others; if he is always unkind: then he is called ill-behaved.”
525.explanation: Mahavira closes his list of the faults of the ill-behaved monk with two failures: not sharing and unkindness.
525.tie_back: The Kural names generosity and kind speech as what draws circle after circle of kin; the Jain text names their opposites, not sharing and unkindness, as the marks of the man who has failed.
525.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
525._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It states the negative of the Kural's two virtues and has no reference to kin gathering round, so the match is partial.

526.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice”
526.explanation: These open the list of faults that make a monk ill-behaved, a list that also includes being angry even with friends and not sharing with others.
526.tie_back: The Kural says no one has more people around him than the generous man who does not nurse anger; the Jain text condemns exactly the nursed anger ('perseveres in his wrath') and the refusal to share.
526.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
526._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Both of the Kural's qualities appear in the same list (11.7-9), but the context is monastic discipline, not winning kin.

527.quote_or_event: At the naming feast of the infant Mahavira, his parents sit down in the dining hall together with their friends, relations, kinsmen, agnates, cognates and followers, and they partook, ate, tasted, and interchanged (bits) of a large collation of food, drink, spices, and sweetmeats.
527.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes the royal family not keeping its good fortune to itself but calling all its kin to eat and share at one table.
527.tie_back: Valluvar's crow caws to call its kin and eats with them; the Jain royal house likewise calls its whole kindred to share its food in celebration.
527.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira § 104 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
527._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (the closing phrase is Jacobi's wording, but the entry is marked as a paraphrase). It is a narrative scene, not a moral teaching, and has no crow image.

528.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra teaches four right attitudes rather than one uniform one: friendliness toward all living beings, joy at the sight of the more virtuous, compassion for the afflicted, and equanimity or tolerance toward the insolent and ill-behaved.
528.explanation: Jain ethics asks a person to adjust his inner regard to the condition and merit of each being he meets.
528.tie_back: The Kural advises regarding each person according to his worth instead of treating all alike; the Tattvartha's four attitudes likewise grade one's regard by the other's virtue and situation.
528.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; English rendering at Jain Square)
528._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against an online English rendering. The sutra concerns inner attitudes toward all beings, not a king's distribution of honours among kin, so the fit is partial.

529.quote_or_event: The brothers Bharata and Bahubali, sons of Rishabhanatha, fall out when Bharata demands his brother's submission and they fight; Bahubali renounces the world, but his omniscience comes only once he lets go of the pride that kept him from bowing to his brothers, and Bharata comes to honour him.
529.explanation: In the Jain account the rift between brothers is mended once its cause, pride and possessiveness, has gone.
529.tie_back: The Kural says kin who left over a grievance return of themselves once the cause of the rift is removed; the Bharata-Bahubali story shows estranged brothers reconciled once the pride between them has gone.
529.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra of Hemachandra, Book 1 (Bharata and Bahubali episode) (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
529._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely told Jain story, based on general knowledge. I could not reach the Johnson translation (wisdomlib.org was down), so the details and chapter location are unverified in this session. Versions differ on whether Bahubali's sister or another figure prompts him to give up his pride.

530.quote_or_event: Jain monastic discipline includes upasthapana, or re-initiation: a monk who has seriously lapsed, or who comes back after leaving, is not simply restored but must undergo expiation and be ordained again.
530.explanation: The Tattvartha Sutra lists re-initiation among the kinds of expiation (prayascitta) by which the community deals with a monk who has broken with it.
530.tie_back: The Kural advises the king to meet the returning kinsman's need but weigh him before taking him back; Jain discipline likewise readmits the returner only after a deliberate process.
530.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.22 (kinds of expiation, including upasthapana) (various translations)
530._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of standard doctrine; I did not verify the wording or the exact sutra numbering in this session. It concerns monks, not kin or kings; next-best match.
